description: The pleasure of testing your ability against a rival under rules built to make the contest fair, so that whoever wins has clearly shown superiority in one quality such as speed, memory or ingenuity.
books: Roger Caillois, Man, Play and Games
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, Flow
Macklin and Sharp, Games, Design and Play

terms: alea; games of chance; games of chance and uncertainty
description: The pleasure of leaving the result to luck: waiting, hoping and risking a stake, with no skill able to change the outcome. In the milder sense Macklin and Sharp give, the pleasure of planning around unpredictable events.
books: Roger Caillois, Man, Play and Games
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, Flow
Macklin and Sharp, Games, Design and Play

description: The pleasure of accepting a pretended world, or of behaving as someone other than yourself, so that you feel more than your ordinary self through fantasy, disguise or pretence.
books: Roger Caillois, Man, Play and Games
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, Flow
Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

description: The pleasure of deliberately unsettling your balance or perception, a short voluptuous panic in an otherwise clear mind, through spinning, falling, speed or other dizziness.
books: Roger Caillois, Man, Play and Games
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, Flow
McKenzie Wark, Gamer Theory

description: The unplanned pleasure of free, noisy, improvised play with no purpose but itself, such as a kitten with wool or a baby with a rattle, tending to run to excess. Boyd names the same ground as spontaneity (acting freely as a whole person) plus exhilaration (a lift that is more than mere excitement).
books: Roger Caillois, Man, Play and Games
Neva Boyd, Play and Game Theory in Group Work

description: The pleasure of working against a difficulty that has been set up for its own sake, an obstacle and not an opponent, and of reaching a satisfactory solution for no other reward.
books: Roger Caillois, Man, Play and Games
Elias, Garfield and Gutschera, Characteristics of Games
Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

sources.their_term: enjoyment of mental or physical challenge

terms: skill-based play; satisfaction from playing well
description: The satisfaction of developing and using skill, whether quick bodily skill (timing, precision) or mental skill (planning, analysis), and of playing well in itself.
books: Macklin and Sharp, Games, Design and Play
Elias, Garfield and Gutschera, Characteristics of Games

terms: fun (as pattern learning); climbing the heuristics tree
description: The pleasure of absorbing a pattern, understanding something new or seeing yourself improve, which the brain rewards. Koster restricts the word fun to this; Burgun and Elias describe the same pleasure as mastery or self-improvement over many plays.
books: Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design
Keith Burgun, Game Design Theory
Elias, Garfield and Gutschera, Characteristics of Games

description: Complete absorption in an activity in which the challenge meets your skill, done for its own sake, with self-consciousness and sense of time dropping away.
books: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, Flow
Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design
Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken

description: Enjoyable hard work: choosing a demanding task so that the stress you feel is energising and optimistic, not fearful, and leaves you stronger than you started.
books: Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken
Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

description: Relaxing, low-effort enjoyment such as passive entertainment. McGonigal argues it leaves people feeling lower than hard fun does; Csikszentmihalyi's 'pleasure' is the same ground, contentment from needs being met, which restores order but does not make you grow.
books: Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, Flow
Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

description: The surge of triumph after overcoming a real difficulty, often shown with arms thrown up. The harder the obstacle, the stronger it is. Elias lists the plain pleasure of winning as a reward.
books: Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken
Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design
Elias, Garfield and Gutschera, Characteristics of Games

terms: the hope of being successful; urgent optimism
description: The feeling of confidence that you can succeed and are improving, and the charged moment of hope just before success when you try hardest.
books: Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken

sources.their_term: the experience, or at least the hope, of being successful

description: The bursting pride of seeing someone you taught or helped succeed, for example coaching a friend through a game you have mastered. Koster adds kvell, the feeling of bragging about someone you mentor.
books: Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken
Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

description: Playful teasing and trash-talking that stings a little and, because it is plainly not meant to hurt, confirms trust and warms the relationship.
books: Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken

description: The pleasure of seeing a rival fail, in effect a put-down.
books: Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

description: The pleasure of working with others towards a shared goal, in step with them and doing what none of you could alone, like a pass that leads to a goal.
books: Macklin and Sharp, Games, Design and Play

terms: social interaction; social connection; people factor
description: The pleasure of the company of other players: talk, give and take, belonging and the bonds that form around a game, before and after as well as during it.
books: Elias, Garfield and Gutschera, Characteristics of Games
Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken
Germaine and Wake, Material Game Studies
Neva Boyd, Play and Game Theory in Group Work

sources.their_term: enjoyment of social interactions during the game
joy of another who has made a good play

terms: the well-played game; playing well together
description: Satisfaction in how a group plays, judged by the manner of playing together, not by who wins; choosing and changing games to suit what all are willing to play, and competing as a loving challenge to each other.
books: Bernie DeKoven, The Well-Played Game

description: The pleasure of social give-and-take in a game: persuading, forming and breaking alliances and bargaining.
books: Elias, Garfield and Gutschera, Characteristics of Games

sources.their_term: social interaction, give-and-take, alliance making and breaking

description: The satisfaction of standing, ranking or being seen as skilled within a group, including records of who won and by how much.
books: Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design
Elias, Garfield and Gutschera, Characteristics of Games

terms: aesthetic appreciation; delight; sensawunda; aesthetic enjoyment
description: The brief pleasure of recognising a pattern and being surprised by it, such as the end of a mystery when everything falls into place. Elias uses aesthetic enjoyment for the look of the game, its graphics and well-made pieces.
books: Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design
Elias, Garfield and Gutschera, Characteristics of Games
Johan Huizinga, Homo Ludens

terms: aesthetic striving play; functional beauty; harmony of practical fit
description: The pleasure of acting, deciding or solving well: the elegance of a clean solution or a perfectly dodged obstacle, and the fit between your abilities and the task.
books: C. Thi Nguyen, Games: Agency as Art

description: The pleasure of handling the components: the weight of chess pieces, the feel of shuffling cards, rolling dice, punching out cardboard, a well-carved game piece.
books: Germaine and Wake, Material Game Studies
Elias, Garfield and Gutschera, Characteristics of Games
Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

terms: excitement or adrenaline rush; visceral reactions
description: The bodily charge of fast, physical or risky play, such as an adrenaline rush, or the physical reactions of mastering a bodily problem.
books: Elias, Garfield and Gutschera, Characteristics of Games
Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

description: The relief of stepping out of everyday life and its cares for a time.
books: Elias, Garfield and Gutschera, Characteristics of Games
Germaine and Wake, Material Game Studies

description: The pleasure of exploring a world or a space of possibilities, finding out how it works and what is in it, and of the sense of discovering something new.
books: Macklin and Sharp, Games, Design and Play
Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, Flow
Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken
Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

description: The satisfaction of belonging to, and contributing to, something larger and longer-lasting than yourself, felt with curiosity, awe and wonder at large scales.
books: Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken

description: The pleasure of a story unfolding through your actions, whether you take on a character in a loose rule-set or move through a designed narrative.
books: Macklin and Sharp, Games, Design and Play

description: The pleasure of acting, improvising and putting on a show, often as much fun to watch as to play, such as charades or a physical dance of bodies.
books: Macklin and Sharp, Games, Design and Play

description: The pleasure of expressing a feeling or idea through a game, as the maker or as the player.
books: Macklin and Sharp, Games, Design and Play
Neva Boyd, Play and Game Theory in Group Work
Raph Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design

description: The pleasure of playing inside a model of a real system, for example as mayor or tycoon, and seeing its workings and the point of view it takes.
books: Macklin and Sharp, Games, Design and Play

description: The strain of an undecided outcome: wanting something to succeed or resolve and striving to decide it, strongest in contests and gambling.
books: Johan Huizinga, Homo Ludens

description: Complete absorption and devotion in play that passes into elation and abolishes the sense of 'only' playing; frivolity and ecstasy are the poles between which play moves.
books: Johan Huizinga, Homo Ludens

terms: whimsical play; silliness; the pleasure of silliness
description: The pleasure of silly actions, unexpected results and absurdity, a sense of euphoria that has to be felt to be understood; for DeKoven also a shared joke, savoured between players.
books: Macklin and Sharp, Games, Design and Play
Bernie DeKoven, The Well-Played Game

description: The enjoyment of failing in an entertaining way, when failure shows your agency, makes you laugh and keeps hope and learning going.
books: Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken

description: The pleasure of being immersed in clear, demanding work that gives quick, visible results.
books: Jane McGonigal, Reality Is Broken

description: The satisfaction of goals that are clear, comparable and rankable, offering relief from the muddle of real-life values.
books: C. Thi Nguyen, Games: Agency as Art

description: Taking up a goal only for the sake of the struggle to reach it, so that the activity is the point and the winning is a device; the reverse of ordinary practical life.
books: C. Thi Nguyen, Games: Agency as Art

description: Plain gladness in play, tending to break out in laughter.
books: Neva Boyd, Play and Game Theory in Group Work
Johan Huizinga, Homo Ludens

description: Playing against the expected script: acting out the forbidden or unexpected, redressing or reskinning, or rewriting the rules, in order to question conventions.
books: Mary Flanagan, Critical Play

description: The excitement of play that comes from the precarious meeting of inner reality and the real, shared world, Winnicott's account of children's playing.
books: D. W. Winnicott, Playing and Reality

sources.their_term: playing is inherently exciting and precarious
